d: A pooled vehicle in which investors commit capital that a manager invests for them. The fund owns the investments; investors own interests in the fund and share its gains and losses pro rata, after fees and carry. Private funds are offered privately to eligible investors, not to the public, which is why they escape most retail fund rules.
x: A €100m venture fund with 25 LPs, a 10-year term and four partners investing in seed-stage software companies.
A ₹500 crore SEBI Category II AIF investing in mid-market Indian companies alongside promoters.
s: A family office wants exposure to 20 early-stage startups but has no team to source and monitor them.
It commits €5m to a venture fund. The manager picks and manages the companies; the family office receives quarterly reports and distributions when companies are sold.
A manager wants to accept money from a pension fund, two family offices and a fund of funds for the same strategy.
A single pooled fund keeps one portfolio and one set of terms, so every investor holds the same deals in proportion to its commitment.

d: Investors commit at the start and cannot redeem. Money comes back only when the fund sells investments and distributes proceeds. The fixed life and locked capital let the manager buy illiquid assets and hold them for years. Standard for VC, PE, infrastructure and most private credit.
x: A buyout fund with a 10-year term plus two optional one-year extensions.
A SEBI Category I VC scheme with a 7-year tenure and up to 2 years' extension with investor approval.
s: In year 4 an LP faces a cash squeeze and asks to redeem its interest.
The LPA gives no redemption right. The LP can only sell its interest to a secondary buyer, usually at a discount to NAV and with GP consent.
Markets fall 30% in year 3 and listed funds face redemptions.
The closed-end fund is not forced to sell, so it can wait for a better exit window. LPs see lower marks but no forced selling.

d: A fund that accepts new subscriptions and allows redemptions at set intervals, priced off NAV, with no fixed end. Private-market versions limit redemptions with gates, notice periods and liquidity sleeves. Under AIFMD II, open-ended EU AIFs must select at least two liquidity management tools.
x: A semi-liquid private equity fund offering quarterly redemptions capped at 5% of NAV.
An open-ended core real estate fund with monthly subscriptions and a 90-day redemption notice.
s: Redemption requests reach 12% of NAV in one quarter against a 5% gate.
The manager pays out 5% pro rata and carries the rest forward. Investors who wanted out wait, but remaining investors are protected from fire sales.
A wealth manager wants clients to invest monthly without capital calls.
An evergreen fund suits this: money is invested at once at the current NAV, with no commitment or drawdown mechanics to manage.

d: The usual legal form for a closed-end fund. A general partner manages it and carries unlimited liability; limited partners are passive and can lose no more than their commitment. The partnership is normally tax transparent, so income is taxed in the partners' hands, and the LPA can set economics almost freely.
x: Delaware LP for US funds; Cayman exempted LP for offshore feeders.
Luxembourg SCSp or English private fund limited partnership for European funds.
s: An LP starts suggesting which companies the fund should buy and attends deal meetings.

Taking part in management can put limited liability at risk in some jurisdictions. Most LPAs and local laws list safe-harbour activities (LPAC seats, voting on LPA amendments) that do not count as management.
A pension fund needs to avoid tax at fund level.
A tax-transparent partnership lets income flow through to the pension fund, which is often exempt at home, instead of being taxed in the vehicle first.

d: The default vehicle for US private funds, formed under the Delaware Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act. Delaware law gives near-total freedom of contract, a specialist business court and well-tested case law, which is why US LPs expect it.
x: A US growth equity fund formed as a Delaware LP with a Delaware LLC as general partner.
A Delaware master fund fed by a Cayman feeder for non-US investors.
s: A European manager targets US endowments for Fund II.
Counsel adds a Delaware parallel fund so US LPs can invest in a familiar vehicle, while EU LPs stay in the Luxembourg SCSp.
An LPA is silent on whether the GP owes fiduciary duties.
Delaware allows duties to be modified or limited in the LPA, but the implied covenant of good faith cannot be removed. Careful drafting decides how much protection LPs keep.

d: A limited partnership under the Cayman Islands Exempted Limited Partnership Act, used for offshore funds and feeders. It is tax neutral and familiar to global LPs. Closed-ended Cayman private funds register with CIMA under the Private Funds Act.
x: A Cayman feeder that pools non-US and US tax-exempt investors into a Delaware master.
An Asia-focused buyout fund formed in Cayman for LPs across many countries.
s: A Middle East sovereign fund wants to avoid US tax filings.
It invests through the Cayman feeder rather than the Delaware vehicle, keeping US tax reporting at the feeder or blocker level.
The fund is formed but not registered with CIMA before accepting capital.
Operating an unregistered private fund breaches Cayman law and can lead to fines; registration and audit requirements need to be in the launch plan.

d: An English or Scottish limited partnership designated as a private fund limited partnership since 2017. The designation lists activities LPs can do without losing limited liability and removes capital contribution requirements, making the UK LP usable for modern funds.
x: A London buyout fund formed as an English PFLP.
A Scottish LP used as a carried interest vehicle because it has separate legal personality.
s: An LP wants to sit on the LPAC and vote on conflicts.
The PFLP white list confirms these activities do not count as taking part in management.
A UK manager raising from EU LPs after Brexit.
The UK LP can still be used, but marketing in the EU now relies on national private placement, not the passport.

d: Special limited partnership under Luxembourg law. It has no legal personality, is tax transparent and leaves wide freedom to the LPA, which is why it became the default EU wrapper for private funds. It can be unregulated with an authorised AIFM, or set up as a RAIF.
x: A €300m European buyout fund formed as an SCSp-RAIF with a third-party AIFM.
A carry vehicle formed as an SCSp so team members hold carry through a transparent entity.
s: A first-time manager wants EU-wide marketing without its own AIFM licence.
It forms an SCSp, appoints a third-party Luxembourg AIFM and uses that AIFM's passport to market to professional investors in other EU states.
LPs ask whether the SCSp pays Luxembourg tax on gains.
As a transparent partnership it is generally not subject to corporate income tax; tax arises at partner level, subject to its activities and structure.

d: Luxembourg Reserved Alternative Investment Fund under the Law of 23 July 2016. The CSSF does not approve it as a product, but it must appoint an authorised AIFM, so it launches in weeks and can still use the AIFMD marketing passport. Open only to well-informed investors.
x: An SCSp-RAIF for a European venture fund launched in six weeks.
A SICAV-RAIF with several compartments for different strategies.
s: A sponsor needs to hold first close in two months.
A RAIF avoids CSSF product approval, so timing depends on the AIFM's onboarding and documents, not regulatory review.
A RAIF wants to admit a retail investor with €20,000.
Not possible: RAIF investors must be well-informed (institutional, professional or at least €100,000 / assessed).

d: Luxembourg specialised investment fund under the Law of 13 February 2007, approved and supervised by the CSSF. Used where investors want a fund that is itself regulated. Many sponsors now choose a RAIF instead for speed.
x: A multi-compartment SIF for real estate strategies.
A SIF chosen because a German insurer requires a CSSF-supervised product.
s: An LP's investment policy allows only regulated funds.
A SIF satisfies this where a RAIF might not, at the cost of CSSF approval time.
A sponsor converts a SIF to a RAIF.
The fund drops direct CSSF supervision but must have an authorised AIFM; LP consent and documentation updates are needed.

a: société d'investissement en capital à risque
d: Luxembourg investment company in risk capital under the Law of 15 June 2004, CSSF-approved and limited to risk capital investments. It offers a specific tax regime on income from those investments.
x: A Luxembourg venture capital vehicle structured as a SICAR.
A SICAR-like RAIF that takes the same tax treatment without CSSF product approval.
s: A sponsor wants to include listed blue chips in the portfolio.
A SICAR must invest in risk capital, so plain listed equities may not qualify.
An LP asks whether the SICAR is subject to subscription tax.
SICARs are not subject to subscription tax, unlike many other Luxembourg funds.

d: French professional private equity fund. It is declared to the AMF, not authorised, and must invest at least half its assets in unlisted companies. Open to professional investors, investors subscribing €100,000 or more, and investors from €30,000 who meet experience conditions.
x: A French growth fund formed as an FPCI managed by a Paris AMF-authorised manager.
An FPCI with an ELTIF label to reach retail investors.
s: A private individual wants to invest €50,000 in an FPCI.
Only possible if the individual meets the experience conditions for the €30,000 tier, such as prior direct investing in unlisted companies.
The fund rules omit the statement that the FPCI is not AMF-authorised.
The AMF General Regulation requires that statement; documents must be corrected before marketing.

a: société de libre partenariat, French LP
d: The French limited partnership created in 2015, with a partnership agreement as flexible as an Anglo-Saxon LPA. It has become a standard structure for institutional French private equity and private debt funds.
x: A French buyout fund raising from international LPs through an SLP.
A private debt fund formed as an SLP so it can originate loans under French rules.
s: Foreign LPs are unfamiliar with French fund forms.
An SLP mirrors the LP/GP model they know, which shortens their legal review.
A service provider to the manager wants to invest €20,000.
SLP rules allow investment by people providing services to the AIFM, subject to conditions.

d: An EU product authorisation for long-term private market funds, marketable to retail and professionals across the EU with one passport. ELTIF 2.0 (from January 2024) removed the €10,000 retail minimum, cut the eligible-asset floor to 55% and allows limited redemptions under the 2024 RTS.
x: A Luxembourg ELTIF giving wealth clients access to infrastructure.
A French FPCI with an ELTIF label sold through private banks.
s: A manager wants retail investors in five EU countries.
An ELTIF passport covers retail distribution across the EU, subject to MiFID suitability, instead of five national regimes.
An ELTIF offers redemptions with a one-month notice.
Under the RTS, shorter notice periods require a larger liquid asset pocket; the manager must calibrate liquidity to redemption terms.

d: An EU label for venture funds investing mainly in young unlisted companies. EuVECA funds can be marketed across the EU to professional investors and to others committing at least €100,000 who state they understand the risks.
x: A Dutch seed fund registered as EuVECA to raise from German business angels.
A sub-threshold venture manager using EuVECA to get a marketing passport without a full AIFM licence.
s: A small manager below AIFMD thresholds wants to raise in three EU countries.
Registering as an EuVECA manager gives a passport that a sub-threshold AIFM would not otherwise have.
An angel investor wants to commit €50,000.
Below the €100,000 minimum for non-professionals, so not eligible.

d: A UK authorised open-ended fund for illiquid assets, introduced in 2021, with notice periods of at least 90 days. Aimed at defined contribution pensions and, with restrictions, some retail investors.
x: A UK LTAF holding private equity and infrastructure for DC pension schemes.
A wealth platform offering an LTAF to restricted mass-market investors.
s: A DC scheme wants private markets in its default fund.
An LTAF gives a regulated, open-ended route with long notice periods suited to illiquid assets.
An investor expects daily dealing.
LTAFs require at least 90 days' notice, so they are not daily-dealing products.

a: Monaco FCP, fonds commun de placement
d: Funds created in Monaco under Law 1.339 of 7 September 2007, including mutual funds (FCP) and funds that may hold non-financial assets. They need CCAF authorisation and a Monaco-licensed manager. They have no EU passport.
x: A Monaco FCP managed by a Monaco SAM for local private banking clients.
A Monaco fund holding real estate, permitted since the 2007 reform.
s: A Monaco manager wants to sell its fund to French investors.
Monaco funds have no AIFMD passport; French national rules apply and the manager may need an EU structure instead.
A foreign manager wants Monaco clients without a local fund.
It can distribute a foreign fund only through a CCAF-authorised firm.

a: Cat I, Cat II, Cat III
d: Indian AIFs register in one of three categories. Category I covers venture capital (including angel funds), SME, social impact and infrastructure funds. Category II covers private equity, private credit and anything not in I or III, with no leverage beyond day-to-day needs. Category III covers hedge-style strategies and may use leverage.
x: A seed fund registered as Cat I VC.
A listed long-short fund registered as Cat III.
s: A PE fund wants to borrow to bridge a deal.
Cat II AIFs may borrow only for temporary needs within SEBI limits, not for leverage.
A manager plans a fund that invests in both startups and listed derivatives.
The strategy needs to fit one category; derivatives trading for returns points to Cat III.

d: Under SEBI rules each scheme of an AIF is a separate vehicle with its own investors, corpus, PPM and compliance. One registered AIF trust can launch several schemes over time.
x: Fund I and Fund II as two schemes of the same AIF trust.
A co-investment scheme launched alongside the main scheme.
s: A manager launches a second scheme five years after the first.
The new scheme files its own PPM through a merchant banker and must meet minimum corpus on its own.
An investor in Scheme 1 asks for exposure to Scheme 2 deals.
They are separate pools; the investor must commit to Scheme 2.

d: Most Indian AIFs are irrevocable trusts registered under the Indian Registration Act. The sponsor settles the trust, a trustee holds assets for the contributors, and the trustee appoints the investment manager. Investors sign contribution agreements rather than an LPA.
x: A Cat II AIF trust with a professional trustee company and a Mumbai manager.
A trust deed naming the sponsor as settlor with ₹1 lakh initial settlement.
s: An investor wants to remove the manager.
The trust deed and contribution agreement set how investors can direct the trustee to replace the manager.
Tax authorities ask whether the trust is determinate.
Pass-through for Cat I and II depends on the section 115UB regime; a determinate trust with identifiable beneficiaries matters for tax treatment.

d: An Indian AIF or scheme in which every investor, other than the manager, sponsor and their employees or directors, is an accredited investor. Introduced by the SEBI Third Amendment of November 2025 with lighter regulatory requirements.
x: A Cat II private credit scheme open only to accredited family offices.
An existing scheme converting to AIOF status under SEBI conditions.
s: A manager wants investors below ₹1 crore.
Accredited investors are exempt from the ₹1 crore minimum, so an AIOF can take smaller tickets from them.
A non-accredited investor applies.
It cannot join an AIOF; the manager must use a standard scheme.

a: LVF, large value fund for accredited investors
d: An Indian AIF where each accredited investor commits at least ₹25 crore (reduced from ₹70 crore in November 2025). LVFs get extra flexibility, such as investing up to 50% of investable funds in one company for Cat I and II.
x: A Cat II LVF backed by insurers and large family offices.
An LVF taking a 40% position in one portfolio company.
s: A ₹30 crore investor wants a fund with higher concentration.
An LVF allows up to 50% in one investee company for Cat I/II, against 25% for other schemes.
An investor committing ₹15 crore wants to join.
Below the ₹25 crore LVF minimum, so not eligible for that scheme.

d: A sub-category of Category I AIF that pools accredited investors to back early-stage startups deal by deal. Since 2025 angel funds accept only accredited investors, and the manager's continuing interest is set per deal at the higher of 0.5% of each investment or ₹50,000.
x: An angel network running a SEBI angel fund to formalise syndicates.
A ₹10 crore angel fund investing ₹50 lakh cheques.
s: A non-accredited angel wants to join.
Not allowed since the 2025 changes; only accredited investors.
The manager invests ₹2 crore in a startup.
Its continuing interest for that deal is the higher of 0.5% (₹1 lakh) or ₹50,000, so ₹1 lakh.

d: A fund in the International Financial Services Centre at GIFT City, regulated by IFSCA under the Fund Management Regulations 2025. Schemes are dollar-denominated and used for foreign-currency pooling, outbound investing from India and inbound feeders.
x: A USD feeder at GIFT City pooling NRI and foreign investors into an Indian Cat II AIF.
A GIFT venture capital scheme investing in Indian and overseas startups.
s: A manager needs foreign LPs to invest in Indian startups without onshore currency issues.
A GIFT fund pools dollars offshore-style while staying in India's regulatory system.
A venture capital scheme takes a 51st investor.
IFSCA caps venture capital schemes at 50 investors.

d: A vehicle that pools a group of investors and invests all or most of its money into a master fund. Feeders separate investors by currency, tax status or jurisdiction while the portfolio is held once.
x: A Cayman feeder for non-US investors into a Delaware master.
A GIFT IFSC feeder pooling dollars into an Indian AIF.
s: Japanese LPs want yen-hedged exposure.
A yen feeder with a currency hedge lets them invest without changing the master.
A feeder's expenses differ from the master's.
Feeder-level costs reduce only that feeder's returns, so LPs compare net returns by feeder.

d: Several feeder funds invest into one master fund that holds the portfolio. Investing happens once at master level; each feeder handles its own investors, tax and reporting.
x: A hedge fund with US and offshore feeders into a Cayman master.
A PE fund with a Luxembourg master and feeders for German and Italian insurers.
s: One feeder's investors want a different fee.
Fees can be set at feeder level without changing the master.
The master suffers a loss.
All feeders share it pro rata to their master interest.

d: A separate fund that invests alongside the main fund in every deal, pro rata to size and on the same terms. Used where some investors need a different legal or tax wrapper.
x: A Luxembourg SCSp running in parallel with a Delaware LP.
An Indian AIF and a GIFT fund co-investing pro rata in each deal.
s: The main fund is 70% and the parallel fund 30% of total commitments.
Each deal is split 70/30 and expenses are shared the same way.
The parallel fund's LPs face a tax issue on one deal.
The LPA may let the parallel fund invest through a different holding route, but it should still bear its pro rata share.

d: A vehicle the GP sets up to make a specific investment on behalf of some or all LPs when the main fund cannot hold it efficiently, for legal, tax or regulatory reasons. AIV investors are the same LPs in the same proportions.
x: A US corporation used as an AIV so tax-exempt LPs avoid UBTI on one deal.
A local holding company formed as an AIV for an investment in a country with foreign ownership limits.
s: A deal would create effectively connected income for non-US LPs.
The GP routes those LPs through an AIV with a blocker for that investment.
LPs ask whether AIV returns count toward the fund's waterfall.
Most LPAs aggregate AIVs with the main fund for waterfall and clawback.

d: A special purpose vehicle formed to hold a single investment, or to group co-investors into one line on a company's cap table. SPVs ring-fence one deal's risks, fees and investors.
x: An SPV holding one company's shares for six co-investing LPs.
A deal-by-deal SPV used by a team before raising its first blind pool.
s: A startup wants one line on its cap table instead of 15 angels.
An SPV pools the angels so the company deals with one shareholder.
A first-time team wants a track record before Fund I.
It runs three deal-by-deal SPVs; their results become evidence in the Fund I PPM.

d: An LP invests directly in a specific deal alongside the fund, usually with reduced or no management fee and carry. Offered when a deal is bigger than the fund's concentration limit, and valued by LPs to lower their blended fee rate.
x: Fund takes €8m of a €15m round; two LPs take the other €7m directly.
A sovereign fund co-invests $50m alongside a buyout fund at zero fee, 10% carry.
s: A deal needs €40m but the fund's limit is €25m.
The GP offers the €15m balance to LPs with co-investment rights.
An LP declines co-investments for a year, then demands one.
Allocation follows the GP's co-investment policy; side letters rarely guarantee allocations.

d: A separate pool raised alongside the main fund to invest in deals too large for it, often with lower fees. Some LPs commit to both; the sidecar follows the main fund's deal selection.
x: A $200m sidecar that takes overflow from a $1bn buyout fund's larger deals.
A sidecar where LPs pay 0.5% fee and 10% carry.
s: A large deal needs more equity than the main fund can provide.
The sidecar fills the gap without the GP running a separate co-investment syndication.
Sidecar LPs get worse deals than the main fund.
Allocation policies must be disclosed; LPAC usually reviews them.

d: A new pool raised late in a fund's life to provide follow-on capital to existing portfolio companies when the original fund has run out of reserves. Investors are often the existing LPs, sometimes with new secondary buyers.
x: A VC fund raising a $50m annex in year 7 to support three winners.
An annex fund created during a funding drought to protect pro rata rights.
s: A star company needs follow-on but the fund has no reserves left.
An annex fund allows the GP to keep its position without breaching the LPA's concentration or recycling limits.
Some LPs decline the annex.
Their exposure to those companies is diluted; pricing and conflicts need LPAC review.

d: Additional capital raised from existing LPs late in the investment period to make new investments when the original fund is fully committed but opportunities remain.
x: A growth fund raising a 20% top-up from its own LPs in year 4.
A top-up with lower fees to match the shorter remaining life.
s: The fund is fully deployed in year 3 with a strong pipeline.
A top-up lets existing LPs add capital rather than waiting for Fund II.
A new LP asks to join the top-up.
Typically offered pro rata to existing LPs; outsiders raise conflict questions.

d: A company inserted between the fund and the operating business to hold shares, raise acquisition debt or manage tax. Buyouts often use topco (equity), midco (subordinated debt) and bidco (buyer) layers.
x: A Luxembourg Sàrl holdco owning a Spanish operating company.
Topco / bidco structure for an LBO with senior debt at bidco.
s: Banks want structural seniority over shareholder loans.
Senior debt sits at bidco, closest to the cash flows; shareholder loans sit higher up.
A tax authority challenges a holdco with no staff.
Substance requirements and anti-abuse rules can deny treaty benefits to a shell.

d: A dedicated arrangement for a single large investor, managed to the same or custom strategy, with terms negotiated directly. The investor gets control and fee discounts; the manager gets a large anchor relationship.
x: A sovereign fund's $500m SMA alongside a manager's flagship fund.
A fund of one for an insurer with custom ESG exclusions.
s: An SMA and the main fund both want the same deal.
An allocation policy decides the split; conflicts are disclosed to both.
The SMA investor wants to stop new investments.
SMA agreements often let the investor terminate the investment period at will.

d: A fund that invests in other funds rather than in companies. It gives diversification, access to managers and selection skill, and adds a second layer of fees and carry.
x: A European FoF backing 15 VC funds across vintages.
A government-backed fund of funds such as India's SIDBI Fund of Funds for Startups.
s: A small family office wants exposure to top VC managers with $1m minimums.
A FoF gives access with a smaller cheque but charges its own fee, often around 1% plus carry.
Underlying fund performance is 2.5x net but the FoF delivers 2.1x.
The gap is the FoF's own fees, carry and cash drag.

d: A new vehicle set up by the GP to buy one or more assets from an older fund so they can be held longer. Existing LPs choose to sell at the offered price or roll into the new vehicle; secondary investors fund the purchase.
x: Single-asset CV for a company the GP wants to hold three more years.
Multi-asset CV taking the last five companies from a 2015 fund.
s: The GP is on both sides of the trade.
LPAC consent, a fairness opinion and a competitive price process are expected to manage the conflict.
An LP rolls its interest.
It keeps exposure, now under new terms (often reset carry and fees); selling LPs get cash at the offered price.

d: A corporation placed between certain investors and the fund so that income which would be taxed badly in their hands is taxed at corporate level instead. Common for US tax-exempt and non-US LPs investing in US operating businesses.
x: US tax-exempt LPs using a blocker to avoid UBTI.
Non-US LPs using a blocker to avoid filing US tax returns.
s: An endowment would owe UBTI on a pass-through portfolio company.
The blocker pays corporate tax instead, and the endowment receives dividends that are not UBTI.
Blocker tax reduces returns.
LPs compare after-tax returns; sometimes leverage or exit structuring reduces the leak.

d: A structure where investors commit to consider each deal individually rather than committing blind capital. The sponsor shows each deal; investors opt in or out. Used by first-time teams to build a record.
x: Five family offices backing a sponsor deal by deal for small buyouts.
A pre-Fund I programme of SPVs with a common term sheet.
s: An investor declines two of five deals.
It has no exposure to those two; returns differ by investor.
The sponsor wants to raise Fund I.
Pledge fund results form a credible, attributable track record.
